cur:objects-bewcastle-cross.summary: On the west face of this tall Northumbrian cross shaft, beneath a panel of John the Baptist holding the Lamb of God, Christ stands in an arched niche, his feet resting on the heads of two beasts, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a scroll. Below, a long runic inscription and the figure of a man with a falcon complete the face. The image presents Christ as Judge, recognised and acclaimed even by the creatures of the wilderness.
facts: Wikipedia notes that only the west face carries human figures; Christ is lifted on the heads of two identical creatures, as on the Ruthwell Cross, and is to be understood as 'Christ the Judge recognised by the beasts'.

The cross also bears what is 'by far the earliest English sundial to survive', and Nikolaus Pevsner called the Bewcastle and Ruthwell crosses 'the greatest achievement of their date in the whole of Europe'.
cur:objects-bewcastle-cross.notes: Image is a 1912 black-and-white photograph (Albert S. Cook).

wga:zearly/1/5coptic/painting/1bawit4.summary: The Virgin, wrapped in a dark mantle and haloed in gold, sits frontally on a jewelled, cushioned throne, holding the Christ Child on her lap. The Child, with his own halo, looks out at the viewer and holds a scroll, a sign that he is the Word of God. Apostles stand on either side; their Greek name labels identify Peter on the left and John on the right. Painted in the lower zone of a chapel apse at the monastery of Bawit, the image presents the incarnate Son seated in his mother's lap as on a throne.
facts: WGA describes this as a detail of the lower register of the same apse whose upper register shows Christ enthroned in glory (also in this collection).
The monastery of Apa Apollo at Bawit, founded c. 385/390, flourished in the 6th and 7th centuries; its paintings are now chiefly in the Coptic Museum, Cairo, and the Louvre.
wga:zearly/1/5coptic/painting/1bawit4.notes: Apostle names read from the partially visible Greek labels (ΠΕΤΡΟΣ at left, ΙΩΑΝΝ... at right). Date broadened to 6th–7th century.
